papers.title: Readout failures in superconducting qubits due to TLS-defects in tunnel junctions
papers.abstract: Material defects give rise to parasitic two-level systems (TLS) which present a major source of decoherence in superconducting qubits. Here, we study a strongly coupled TLS that resides in the tunnel barrier of transmon qubit. We use multi-photon spectroscopy and TLS strain tuning to explore the rich spectrum of the interacting three-partite system consisting of TLS, qubit, and its readout resonator. This reveals a strong effective resonant coupling between the TLS and the qubit's readout resonator which dresses the resonator states and results in a resonance frequency shift that spoils the readout signal. Our finding presents yet another way how material defects can interfere with qubit operation and hinder the realization of solid-state quantum processors.

summary.summary: A strongly coupled two-level system (TLS) in a transmon qubit's tunnel junction creates a qubit-mediated effective resonant coupling to the readout resonator via virtual qubit excitations, producing an avoided-level crossing that shifts the resonator frequency and spoils readout fidelity. Multi-photon spectroscopy combined with mechanical strain tuning reveals this mechanism and maps the rich spectrum of the qubit-resonator-TLS system, with effective coupling $g_	ext{eff} = g_r g_x / 	ext{δ}$ reaching 1.5 MHz at 500 MHz detuning.
summary.motivation: TLS defects in Josephson junctions are known to cause qubit decoherence and dropout, but their role in readout errors has been underexplored. Understanding this new failure mechanism is critical for scaling superconducting quantum processors where TLS in tunnel barriers occur at densities of 100–8000 TLS/(GHz·μm³).
summary.method: Spectroscopy of an Al/Si transmon with $f_q^{	ext{max}} = 7.32$ GHz was performed while tuning a strongly coupled TLS ($g_x = 21.7$ MHz, $\bar{p}_0 = 0.36$ e Å) through resonance via mechanical strain ($\gamma = 212$ MHz/V) applied to the qubit chip, combined with QuTiP simulations of the full three-level system including multi-photon transitions.
summary.result: The parasitic TLS-resonator coupling creates a resonance frequency shift comparable to the dispersive readout signal ($\chi \approx g_r^2/\text{δ}$), directly causing readout failure when the TLS is tuned into resonance with the 6.625 GHz resonator; this occurs with probability ~0.1–2 TLS/GHz for typical small-area junctions.

papers.title: Opportunities and challenges in scaling quantum error detection on hardware
papers.abstract: Quantum error detection can produce unbiased expectation values that exponentially converge to noiseless results as the code distance is increased. Despite this, its performance as an error mitigation technique is relatively understudied on quantum hardware because of its two main drawbacks: (i) the number of samples increases exponentially in the circuit depth/noise level, and (ii) the classical processing generally grows exponentially in the code distance, though exceptions exist. Additionally, the constant (but often large) overhead of embedding the code and logical operations on hardware can make accuracy worse instead of better. In this work, we seek to provide a clear picture of these opportunities and challenges for scaling quantum error detection on hardware. We do so by performing a detailed benchmarking study on real and simulated noisy quantum computers, using the repetition code and triangular color code for memory experiments and logical computations with up to $74$ physical qubits. In addition to these benchmarks, we estimate the pseudothreshold of codes to map the frontier of error detection on current and future quantum computers. Despite the challenges, our results show strong promise for scaling quantum error detection on hardware.

summary.summary: This paper presents a detailed benchmarking study of quantum error detection on IBM quantum computers using the repetition code and triangular color code, demonstrating exponential convergence of expectation values to noiseless results as code distance increases up to 74 physical qubits. The work characterizes the practical challenges of sampling overhead and classical post-processing, and identifies pseudothresholds below which error detection outperforms unencoded circuits.
summary.motivation: Quantum error detection is an unbiased error mitigation technique that can improve accuracy with additional spatial resources, but its scaling properties on real hardware have been relatively understudied despite two major drawbacks: exponential sampling overhead in circuit depth and exponential classical processing in code distance.
summary.method: Experiments performed on IBM quantum computers (Kyiv, Fez, Boston) implementing repetition codes ($[n,1,n]$) for memory experiments and logical Bell state preparation, and triangular color codes ($[n,1,d]$ with $n = (3d^2+1)/4$) at distances $d=3,5,7$ corresponding to 14, 38, and 74 physical qubits, with up to 3146 two-qubit gates and dynamical decoupling.
summary.result: For the repetition code memory experiment, $\langle \bar{Z} \rangle$ converges exponentially to the ideal value as $n$ increases, consistent with the theoretical prediction $\langle \bar{O} \rangle(n) = p^D \mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\rho}\bar{O}]/(p^D + (1-p^D)/2^{n-1})$; triangular color code experiments show better-than-physical performance at distance 3 for all depths and identify a pseudothreshold $p^*$ that decreases exponentially with circuit depth $D$.
